content: Componentwise weak convergence of signed synaptic kernels alone does not determine the fast-synapse limit of a sparse threshold-reset network. Within a causal event protocol featuring clamped refractoriness and smooth positive-delay kernels, we construct two families whose excitatory and inhibitory measures both converge weakly to $δ_0$, yet differ in the microscopic order of spike arrivals. In the excitatory-first family, the target neuron fires; in the inhibitory-first family, it does not. This distinction arises precisely when $x+a-b<θ\le x+a$. Strict margins ensure this response is robust to perturbations in the target state, aggregate E/I pulse masses, and bounded drift. This macroscopic effect persists on a moderately sparse, Dale-compatible random block graph with $q_N\to\infty$ and $q_N/N\to0$, where both systems share the same graph and initial data. Along any deterministic joint scaling $\varepsilon_N\downarrow0$, their population-averaged firing counts differ by $1/2+o_{L^1}(1)$. A bounded-degree construction and subsequent probe demonstrate that this discrepancy is macroscopic and can persist through reset. Fixed positive-delay kernels with finitely many classes admit a stable regime: before grazing, typewise-mixing sparse networks converge to a delayed class mean-field system. For directed Erdős–Rényi graphs, the bound $O_P(λ_N^{-1/2}+\|π_N-π\|_1)$ holds when $λ_N\to\infty$ and $λ_N/N\to0$. This result separates stable averaging at fixed delay from singular collapse; in the latter, componentwise weak convergence loses the signed arrival-order information essential for the threshold-reset response.
